items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the real property tax law, in relation to providing that a
certain time limit for purposes of qualifying for a tax abatement shall not
apply to certain brand-new from the ground up construction sited on property
purchased from the city of New York
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5882

SPONSOR: PERSAUD
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the real property tax law, in relation to providing that
a certain time limit for purposes of qualifying for a tax abatement
shall not apply to certain brand-new from the ground up construction
sited on property purchased from the city of New York

 
PURPOSE:

To ensure that certain brand-new from the ground up construction, sited
on certain property purchased from the City of New York which would
qualify as an Industrial & Commercial Abatement Program (ICAP) eligible
economic development project and for which the planned construction was
pursued based on an expectation that the ICAP benefit would help defray
future economic liabilities such as higher property taxes assessed
resulting from the new construction, shall not be denied eligibility or
denied approval based solely on the date of receipt of the final appli-
cation when all other qualifying conditions have been met.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill adds subparagraph (iii) to paragraph (a) of
subdivision 5 of § 489-cccccc of the real property tax law to exempt
brand-new construction from the ground up located on property purchased
from the city of New York for the purposes of an eligible development
pursuant to this article wherein the sales agreement includes a
restriction preventing the sale or transfer of the property for a period
of five years or more, and where the first valuation and assessment for
the purposes of property taxes occurred within that period of
restriction from sale from the time limit to file a final application to
receive the benefits of the industrial and commercial abatement program
projects provided the project meets all other requirements of the indus-
trial and commercial abatement program.

Section two of the bill provides the .effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Administered by the New York City Department of Finance, ICAP seeks to
incentivize economic activity by providing property tax abatements when
a business constructs a new building or provides an overall improvement
to a commercial or industrial building. The requirements to participate
in ICAP are multifaceted and include an application process that
requires the filing of a preliminary application followed by the
submission of a final application within one year from the date of issu-
ance of the first building permit or, if no permit is required, the
commencement of construction.Failure to submit the final application
within what has been described as a hard one-year time limit, starting
from the date of issuance of first building permit, and for a building
requiring no permit, starting from the commencement of construction,
does result in automatic disqualification.

Over the life of the ICAP program, the problem with this summary
disqualification is that it is often too severe a punishment for missing
a timeline when dealing with the very complicated process of building
construction in the City of New York.The complexity of the building and
construction process, which may include several applications for a
multitude of permits from several different agencies, all within a
twelve month period, makes for a perilous and daunting undertaking that
forces applicants to increase their costs by having to hire specialists
to successfully navigate down that road to meet the narrow one year
timeline. No wonder the history of the program shows that many busi-
nesses end up missing that deadline and get stuck with high real estate
taxes, sometimes too high for their budget to accommodate.  Also signif-
icant, especially for brand new from the ground up buildings that come
with first time valuation and assessments, is the fact that the actual
cost of the property tax was not predictable prior to completion of the
building.

As such, the promise of ICAP can turn out to be a costly debt to the
business. Businesses that fail to qualify and end up with an unplanned
and unbudgeted high real estate property tax assessment that comes due
immediately and reoccurs each year thereafter should always have the
freedom to choose the best option to manage or bail out of the business
with no limitations as to what actions they can take alleviate the
financial consequences. Among those options should be the freedom to
sell the new property at the best market rate if that is a viable option
for the business.

So where the promise and expectation of the ICAP benefit clearly serves
as an incitive and attraction to the developer to make the construction
investment, it is certainly an appearance of unjustifiable unfairness to
be denied the benefit and at the same time being restricted and denied
the option of choosing a reasonable financial exit, such as selling the
new building. Certainly, a developer who ends up in this situation could
complain of being trapped, which is not the intent of the ICAP program,
and the rules adopted to operate the program as a financial incentive
for economic development.

ICAP is intended to stimulate economic growth by, amongst other things,
encouraging new construction projects. ICAP has been utilized for a
number of years and the program has been found to be mutually beneficial
to property owners and the City of New York. This legislation will
rectify situations such as these to the benefit of not only the property
owner, but also to the community in which the business is located
through increased economic activity and growth.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately and shall apply to projects for which a final application
for benefits was filed on and after January 1, 2018.
